subject: How even or uneven the coverage probability should be in simulated designs?

messages.author: 512996ea4ff0ea65
messages.subject: How even or uneven the coverage probability should be in simulated designs?
parts:
Hi everybody, maybe this was answered long ago but maybe not.

When analyzing designs in DISTANCE, how uneven should be the coverage probability for considering a design "unsuitable"? 

I ask if there is a rule of thumb, for example if there is an order of magnitud between the minimum and the maximum, if more than 2 or 3 times between the minmum and maximum.... I found nothing searchng the web...

Also I wonder how dependent is the coverage probability on the number of simulations executed. I explored the supplemental material of Thomas et al. 2007 (Designing line transect surveys for complex survey regions), and went int the Design named 1, for the parallel designs of 36 km . The map of coverage probability is quite different if you see the 1000 simulations against the 10000 simulations...so maybe it is alway better to simulate 10000 times?

Many thanks

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How even or uneven the coverage probability should be in simulated designs?
parts:
Adrian:

Interesting questions, as always.

The simple answer is that evenness of coverage probability is subjective.  There is no objective measure of evenness, although Strindberg did look at some metrics in her thesis.  Think of the analogy of a QQ plot as a measure of goodness of fit.  How far can the QQ plot deviate from the 45-degree line before you decide your model does not fit your data?  That is a subjective judgement, which is why the K-S and CvM tests quantify the visual image shown in the QQ plot.

I would not use the range (max - min) as a measure of evenness.  My personal preference is to use the standard deviation of hit percentage as an index of evenness.  I can use this as a relative measure "does design A produce more even coverage than design B".

With the highly crenelated study area of Thomas et al. (2007), I don't doubt that very large numbers of simulations may be needed to get a reasonable assessment of coverage probability.
